trivia_fact: Kubernetes mandates that every pod gets its own unique IP address and that all pods can communicate without NAT. This "flat networking" model was a deliberate simplification — it avoids the port-mapping complexity that plagued Docker's default bridge networking.

The Container Network Interface (CNI) standard was created by CoreOS in 2015 to decouple container runtimes from networking implementations. Kubernetes adopted CNI to let operators choose their networking stack without changing any cluster code.

Project Calico is named after the calico cat — a multi-colored cat breed. The metaphor is that Calico weaves together multiple networking capabilities (routing, policy, encryption) into one colorful solution.

Flannel, created by CoreOS, was one of the first and simplest CNI plugins. It uses a single flat layer-3 network and assigns each node a subnet. Its simplicity made it the default choice for learning environments, though production clusters often outgrow it.

kube-proxy runs on every node to implement the Service abstraction. It originally used userspace proxying, then switched to iptables rules, and now supports IPVS mode for high-scale clusters. Despite the name, it is not a traditional proxy — it programs kernel-level packet forwarding rules.

The Kubernetes Service was designed to solve the "discovery and load balancing" problem for ephemeral pods. Because pods come and go with new IPs, Services provide a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) that never changes, even as the backend pods are replaced.

The three core Service types form a hierarchy: ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (extends ClusterIP by opening a port on every node), and LoadBalancer (extends NodePort by provisioning a cloud load balancer). Each type builds on the one below it.

The Ingress resource, added in Kubernetes 1.1, was always considered limited — it only handled HTTP routing with a single spec that different controllers interpreted differently. The Gateway API (graduated to GA in 2023) replaced it with a more expressive, role-oriented model separating infrastructure from application concerns.

Kubernetes replaced kube-dns with CoreDNS as the default cluster DNS in version 1.13 (2018). CoreDNS is a CNCF graduated project written in Go with a plugin architecture that makes it more flexible and easier to extend than the previous kube-dns stack.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources act as pod-level firewalls. By default, all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed. NetworkPolicies are "deny by addition" — once you apply a policy selecting a pod, all non-matching traffic to that pod is denied. The CNI plugin must support NetworkPolicy for enforcement.

Cilium is a CNI plugin that uses eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) to implement networking, security, and observability directly in the Linux kernel. This bypasses iptables entirely, offering significant performance improvements at scale. Cilium became a CNCF graduated project in 2023.

A "headless" Service (ClusterIP set to None) skips the load-balancing proxy entirely and returns the individual pod IPs directly via DNS. This is essential for stateful workloads like databases where clients need to connect to specific pods, not a random one behind a VIP.
